value.overview: The Marbled Wood-Quail is a secretive, ground-dwelling member of the New World quail family. It lives mainly in humid tropical forest, where its richly patterned brown plumage provides excellent camouflage among leaf litter and dense undergrowth. Usually detected by its loud, repeated calls rather than seen, it may occur alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. Costa Rica represents the northern part of its distribution, with records primarily from suitable lowland Pacific forests.
value.classification: The Marbled Wood-Quail belongs to the family Odontophoridae, the New World quails, within the order Galliformes. Its scientific name is Odontophorus gujanensis.
value.identification: This medium-sized wood-quail measures about 23–29 cm. Both sexes are similar, with predominantly brown, grayish-brown, and buff plumage marked by fine black barring and vermiculations. It has a short, loose crest, a reddish-brown head, a chestnut chin, and a pale throat finely barred with dark markings. The bare skin around the eye is bright orange-red, an especially useful field mark. Its dark bill and greenish-gray legs contrast with the warm tones of the plumage.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad range from Costa Rica and Panama through Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, and parts of Ecuador. It inhabits humid lowland evergreen forest, forest undergrowth, older secondary woodland, and other dense, shaded habitats, generally from sea level to about 900 m, with higher records elsewhere in South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species associated mainly with humid lowland Pacific forest, including the Osa-Golfo Dulce region and Carara, where it can persist in intact or suitable regenerating forest.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and presumed sedentary. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round rather than being a seasonal migrant, although its local detectability may vary with weather, breeding activity, and forest conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited and may vary across its large range. The species is believed to form monogamous pairs, and the nest is a shallow ground scrape concealed beneath fallen leaves or other cover; some nests may be placed near the base of a tree or in a sheltered cavity. Clutches commonly contain about four pale eggs, sometimes with light staining or spots. Incubation is reported to last roughly 26–27 days in captivity, but details of wild nesting in Costa Rica remain sparse.
value.dietFeeding: The Marbled Wood-Quail feeds on the forest floor, taking fallen fruits, berries, seeds, nuts, and other plant material. It probably supplements this diet with insects and other small invertebrates, especially when feeding chicks. Birds scratch through leaf litter and soil while moving quietly through dense cover. Its terrestrial feeding habits make undisturbed ground vegetation and a continuous supply of fallen food important components of its habitat.
value.behavior: This is a shy, wary, and predominantly terrestrial bird that usually escapes by running into dense cover, flying only when closely pressed. It is often encountered in pairs or small groups. Early morning is the best time to hear it, when pairs or groups give loud, repeated, coordinated calls or duets. The species is difficult to observe because it stays low in thick vegetation, but its distinctive vocalizations can carry considerable distances through forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the rate and extent of decline are not well quantified. It remains locally common or fairly common where suitable forest is protected, including parts of Costa Rica.
conservation.threats: The principal concerns are loss and fragmentation of humid tropical forest, conversion of lowland woodland to agriculture or pasture, and hunting in some parts of its South American range. In Costa Rica, maintaining large areas of connected lowland forest is especially important because the species depends on dense ground cover and is not well suited to heavily cleared landscapes.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore lowland rainforest and mature secondary forest, maintain habitat corridors, and reduce further fragmentation. In Costa Rica, support conservation of Pacific lowland forests such as those in the Osa-Golfo Dulce region and Carara. Avoid disturbing calling or feeding birds, keep dogs under control near forest edges, and contribute well-documented sightings and sound recordings to responsible bird-monitoring programs.
